prompt.context: Our client is a supermarket chain. We are looking at their deli department, which sells both deli meats and prepared foods. Despite overall deli revenue growing from $620M to $700M over the past two years, overall gross margin (profit) has remained flat at $270M. The client has asked us to help them understand why profits are not growing and what they should do about it.
prompt.question: What should the supermarket do to turn around its deli department?

clarifying_info.q: What is happening in the overall deli industry?
clarifying_info.a: The deli meat category has been flat to slightly declining recently. The prepared foods category has been growing at roughly 10% per year as people have less time to cook at home.

There is increasing competition from deli departments of other supermarkets and discounters, which are expanding product lines and increasing advertising. The prepared foods segment also competes with fast food restaurants.

clarifying_info.q: Has the client's product mix changed recently?
clarifying_info.a: Mix has remained constant, with the exception of two products introduced a couple of years ago: BBQ chicken wings and 'made to order' sandwiches. Both products have been a major boost to prepared foods revenue.

clarifying_info.q: What are the revenues of the new products?
clarifying_info.a: Revenues for each product are $40M annually. Costs are not broken down at the product level.

exhibits.title: Supermarket Deli Turnaround — Financial Summary
exhibits.shows: A table of revenues and COGS (in $M) for Deli Meats, Prepared Foods, and Overall, across years 2002, 2003, and 2004

exhibits.title: Supermarket Deli Turnaround — New Product Details
exhibits.shows: Unit economics data for two new products: BBQ wings and made-to-order sandwiches, including price, material cost, prep/employee time, and per-store daily financials

framework: Break down revenues and profits by segment (deli meats vs. prepared foods) to isolate where the problem lies
Analyze whether flat profits are driven by flat revenues, rising costs, or declining margins within each segment
Identify root causes: changes in product/sales mix, rising material costs, rising labor costs
Evaluate new products (BBQ wings, made-to-order sandwiches) and their individual unit economics
Assess external environment: category trends and competitive dynamics
Develop recommendations addressing the root cause, with consideration of second-order effects (store traffic)

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, which part of the deli business is responsible for the lack of profit growth — deli meats, prepared foods, or both?
questions.guidance: Deli meat revenues are essentially flat (~$260M), consistent with the flat industry category; COGS also flat, so deli meat gross profit is flat but not deteriorating. Prepared foods revenues are growing ~10% per year ($360M → $400M → $440M), consistent with the category, but COGS are growing faster ($190M → $230M → $270M), so prepared foods gross profit is flat. The problem is concentrated in prepared foods: revenue is growing but margins are deteriorating.

math.setup: Calculate gross profit for each segment each year
steps: Prepared foods gross profit: 360-190=170, 400-230=170, 440-270=170 → flat despite 10% revenue growth
math.answer: Prepared foods gross margin is declining from ~47% to ~39% even as revenue grows; the root cause of flat total profits lies entirely in prepared foods.

questions.prompt: What are some potential reasons for the deteriorating margins in prepared foods?
questions.guidance: A strong answer considers three buckets: (1) Change in product/sales mix toward lower-margin items; (2) Rising material costs (ingredient inflation); (3) Rising labor costs. The candidate should probe product mix changes first, since the interviewer has hinted at two new products.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the profitability of BBQ chicken wings and made-to-order sandwiches. Which product, if any, is causing the margin problem?
questions.guidance: BBQ wings: material cost $0.10/piece, prep time 15 min per batch of 200 (0.075 min/piece), employee cost $20/hr = $0.025/piece labor → total COGS $2.50 per 20 pieces vs. revenue $5 per 20 pieces → 50% margin. BBQ wings are profitable and not the problem. Made-to-order sandwiches: revenue $4 × 20 = $80/store/day; labor 4 hrs × $20 = $80, material $2 × 20 = $40, total COGS = $120/store/day; margin = $80 - $120 = –$40/store/day. The client is losing money on every store that offers made-to-order sandwiches.

math.setup: BBQ wings unit economics and sandwich store-level P&L
steps: BBQ wings: material = 20 × $0.10 = $2.00; prep labor = (15/60) hr per 200 pieces × $20 = $0.025 per piece × 20 = $0.50; total COGS = $2.50 per 20 pieces; revenue = $5.00; margin = $2.50 (50%)
math.answer: BBQ wings earn a 50% margin and are not the issue. Made-to-order sandwiches lose $40 per store per day; they are the root cause of deteriorating prepared foods margins.

brainstorming.prompt: What recommendations would you make to address the made-to-order sandwich problem? Consider multiple levers.

categories.name: Eliminate or restrict the product
ideas: Eliminate made-to-order sandwiches entirely across all stores
Restrict to higher-traffic stores where volume can cover the fixed labor cost
Restrict hours to peak demand periods only (e.g., lunch hours only instead of both lunch and dinner)

categories.name: Pricing adjustments
ideas: Raise sandwich price to improve margin per unit (test demand elasticity first)
Lower price to drive volume — only viable if labor cost is largely fixed and additional volume tips the store P&L positive

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Reduce dedicated labor hours (e.g., one employee handling sandwiches plus light deli tasks rather than fully dedicated)
Negotiate lower ingredient costs through supplier contracts or simpler ingredient list
Streamline sandwich menu to reduce prep complexity

categories.name: Demand stimulation
ideas: Increase advertising and in-store promotions to drive more sandwiches sold per day
Improve merchandising and placement to increase visibility
Partner with corporate accounts or offices nearby for bulk orders

categories.name: Second-order / traffic effects
ideas: Consider whether removing made-to-order sandwiches reduces foot traffic to the deli and broader store
Evaluate whether the sandwich concept builds brand differentiation worth a short-term loss
Track impact on overall basket size for customers who use the sandwich station

recommendation: Immediately restrict or eliminate the made-to-order sandwich program in low-traffic stores and during non-peak hours (dinner), as these locations are generating losses with insufficient volume to cover the fixed $80/day labor cost

In higher-traffic stores and during peak lunch hours, test a price increase or reduced labor model to determine whether the product can reach breakeven; maintain BBQ wings program as a profitable growth driver consistent with the prepared foods trend
risks: Eliminating made-to-order sandwiches may reduce store traffic and hurt overall deli and store revenue — must monitor basket size and visit frequency
Raising prices may reduce volume and worsen the loss if demand is elastic
Cutting dedicated labor hours may hurt quality and customer experience
next_steps: Conduct a store-level analysis to identify which stores and time windows have sufficient sandwich volume to cover the $80/day fixed labor cost (breakeven = 26.7 sandwiches/store/session at $4 price and $2 material cost)
Pilot a price increase (e.g., $5/sandwich) in select stores and measure volume impact
Evaluate whether a part-time or shared employee model can reduce labor cost below $80/day while maintaining service quality
